posts.content_html:
Shopify vs Squarespace comes down to what you're building. Short answer: Shopify wins for ecommerce stores built to grow, while Squarespace wins for design-led sites with small, curated catalogs. If selling products is the core of your business, Shopify's catalog capacity, payment options, and app ecosystem give it a clear edge. If your shop is a side of a portfolio or service business, Squarespace can be the better fit. Below we compare both, show the signs you've outgrown Squarespace, and explain how an ecommerce platform migration to Shopify works when it's time to move.

Shopify vs Squarespace at a Glance

AreaShopifySquarespace

Payments100+ providers, plus Shopify Payments and Shop PayA handful of processors
AppsThousands of appsA few dozen extensions

Where Shopify Wins for Ecommerce

Catalog capacity. Shopify has no cap on product count. Squarespace's documented limits are far lower, and growing stores tend to reach them sooner than expected.

Payments and checkout. Shopify connects to more than 100 payment providers, which matters when you sell in new regions or need a specific gateway.

Apps and sales channels. Subscriptions, reviews, loyalty, and marketplace selling are a few clicks away through the Shopify App Store.

Operations. Multi-location inventory and a built-in point-of-sale system support stores that sell in more than one place.

International selling. Squarespace added multi-currency checkout in a 2026 update, though it leaves out subscriptions and digital products. Shopify Markets goes further, managing currency, languages, domains, and pricing by market.

Where Squarespace Still Wins

Squarespace is excellent for brand-first sites. Its templates are polished, the editor is simple, and it blends content, bookings, and a small shop in one place. If you sell a few dozen products, ship low volumes, and treat design as your main differentiator, you may never need more.

Which Should You Choose?

Choose Shopify if:

  • Selling products is your main business
  • You expect your catalog, orders, or markets to grow
  • You want marketplace, subscription, or advanced inventory options

Choose Squarespace if:

  • Your brand and design matter more than commerce depth
  • You sell a small, curated range
  • Your shop supports a service or content business

Signs You've Outgrown Squarespace

  • You're approaching product or variant limits
  • Customers ask for payment methods you can't offer
  • You want to sell on marketplaces or run advanced inventory
  • Your marketing needs apps that Squarespace doesn't have
  • You're expanding into new countries

What Migration to Shopify Involves

A Shopify store migration from Squarespace moves your data, not your design. A proper Shopify data migration carries products and variants, images, customer accounts, orders, blog posts, and pages. Your design gets rebuilt in a Shopify theme, a good chance to modernize it, and customers sign in with an emailed code instead of a password.

The Shopify migration process runs in four stages: connect your store, preview a demo migration, run the full migration while your store stays live, then launch with a final sync and domain switch. Every old URL also needs a 301 redirect to protect your SEO. Any ecommerce migration is only as good as the data it carries across, so check what moves before you commit. Most stores finish the transfer within hours to a few days, as we explain in how long a Shopify migration takes. For product-focused stores that plan to grow, yes. Squarespace suits design-led brands with small catalogs.

Short answer: most of what keeps merchants stuck on a platform they've outgrown is a myth, or a half-truth left over from how migrations used to go. Ecommerce replatforming has a reputation for broken sites, lost rankings, and months of cleanup. Some of that reputation is earned, but mostly by manual projects and weak tools, not by the move itself. Here are five common myths, what's actually true, and where a myth holds a grain of truth worth planning for.

Myth #1: "You'll Lose Your Google Rankings"

This is the biggest fear, and it's only partly a myth. Rankings do drop when old URLs have no redirects and when meta titles and image alt text get left behind. They don't drop simply because you changed platforms. When every old URL gets its own 301 redirect and your SEO data comes along, rankings usually stabilize within a few weeks of launch, and some short-term fluctuation is normal while Google recrawls. Our guide on what actually affects your Google rankings during a Shopify migration breaks this down step by step.

Myth #2: "Your Store Will Be Down for Days"

Manual migrations used to mean a maintenance page and crossed fingers. A zero downtime migration works differently: your original store stays live and keeps taking orders while your data copies to Shopify in the background. At launch, a final sync picks up anything that arrived mid-migration, and then you point your domain at the new store. The part customers could notice is measured in minutes to about an hour, not days. The grain of truth: it's still smart to launch during a quieter week rather than in the middle of a big sale.

Myth #3: "Your Customers Will Have to Start Over"

The honest version is that customers will notice a couple of things. Passwords can't transfer between any two platforms, and Shopify's current customer accounts sign in with an emailed code instead of a password. Saved credit cards live with your payment processor, so they usually only carry over through a processor-level transfer. But accounts, addresses, and order history can all move across, which means no one logs in to an empty account. We cover the details in our guide to migrating customer accounts to Shopify.

Myth #4: "Replatforming Means Rebuilding Everything, and It Takes Months"

This one is half true. Your visual design does not migrate, because Shopify runs on its own theme system, so your new storefront is a separate build. That's also a chance to modernize a layout you've outgrown. But your data does not need rebuilding. Products, customers, orders, blog posts, and pages can all move across, and the transfer itself typically takes anywhere from a couple of hours to three days depending on catalog size. The full project, including planning and testing, usually runs one to three weeks, and a standard migration doesn't require a developer. This is the myth that does the most damage.   • A properly run migration keeps your old store live until the final switch
  • Customer accounts, addresses, and order history can migrate; passwords and saved cards work differently
  • Data transfer takes hours to days, while design is a separate parallel build
  • A complete migration tool does far more than a basic product import

Short answer: you can make the switch invisible where it matters most, and honest about the rest. A well-run move means no downtime, no broken links, no missing orders, and no lost accounts. A few things, like a new look or a different sign-in screen, will be visible, so the goal is to make those feel planned rather than accidental. If you want to switch ecommerce platforms without a flood of confused emails, here is what to protect, what to announce, and how to launch without a hiccup.

What Customers Actually Notice (and What They Don't)

When you switch ecommerce platforms, customers rarely care which platform runs your store. They care about whether the site loads, whether their old links work, whether their order history is still there, and whether checkout feels familiar. Those are the things that make a switch noticeable in the wrong way. Behind the scenes, nobody sees your database moving. The real work of an ecommerce platform migration is keeping those four promises intact while everything underneath changes.

Keep Your Old Store Live Until the Very Last Step

The single biggest reason customers notice when you switch ecommerce platforms is downtime. The fix is a zero downtime migration: your original store keeps taking orders while your data copies across to Shopify in the background. Nothing changes for shoppers until launch day, when a final sync picks up any orders or customers that arrived mid-migration and you point your domain at the new store. If you copy your data first and test it thoroughly, the switch itself takes about an hour instead of a weekend of "we'll be back soon" banners.

Protect the Links Customers Already Have

Shoppers return to your store through bookmarks, old emails, social posts, and Google results. If those links break, customers notice immediately, and so does your search ranking. Every old URL needs a 301 redirect to its new Shopify address. One honest note: Shopify adds fixed prefixes like /products/ to your URLs, so they won't look identical, but a proper redirect sends people to the right page without them ever seeing an error. Carry Over Accounts and Order History

Nothing makes a customer feel a switch like logging in and finding their past orders gone. Passwords are the one thing that cannot move between platforms, but Shopify's current accounts use an email code to sign in instead of a password, which makes the handoff simpler than it used to be. Tell Customers About the Few Things They Will See

Being upfront beats hoping nobody notices. Three changes tend to be visible. First, your design: layouts don't transfer between platforms, so your new theme will look different, and it helps to keep your logo, colors, and fonts consistent. Second, sign-in: customers will enter an emailed code instead of a password. Third, saved payment methods: stored cards live with your payment processor, not your store platform, so they usually only carry over through a direct processor-to-processor transfer, and otherwise customers re-enter them once. A short announcement email a few days before launch turns these from surprises into non-events.

Most migration tools move product listings and stop there. That leaves customer accounts, order history, and redirects as manual cleanup, which is exactly how stores end up with shoppers who can't find their orders and links that lead nowhere.   • Keep your old store live and taking orders until the final sync
  • Confirm every old URL redirects to its new Shopify page
  • Place a test order and check confirmation and shipping emails

Not with a properly run migration. Your original store keeps taking orders while data copies in the background, and the only brief change is the domain switch at launch.

posts.meta_title: How to Tell Google You've Moved After a Shopify Migration
posts.meta_description: Migrated to Shopify? Here's exactly how to tell Google - Search Console setup, sitemap submission, the Change of Address tool, and what to monitor.
posts.content_html:
Short answer: it depends on whether your domain changed, or just your platform did. If you kept the same domain and only switched the software running behind it, Google doesn't need a formal "we moved" declaration - it needs correct redirects, a fresh sitemap, and time to recrawl. If your domain changed too, there's a specific Google Search Console tool built exactly for that. Here's precisely what to do in each case, and the steps people skip that quietly slow down recovery.

First: Did Your Domain Change, or Just Your Platform?

This distinction determines almost everything that follows, and it's the part a lot of migration advice glosses over. If mystore.com stayed mystore.com and you simply moved from Wix or BigCommerce to Shopify underneath it, that's a platform change with no URL-level domain change - Google's Change of Address tool doesn't apply here, and using it incorrectly won't help. If you moved to a different domain entirely (or from a subdomain like mystore.myshopify.com to your own custom domain), that's a domain change, and Google has a dedicated process for it.

👉 See how ShiftItNow handles redirects for your specific migration before you touch Search Console.

If You Kept the Same Domain: What to Actually Do

Re-verify your property in Google Search Console using a method Shopify supports - an HTML meta tag, DNS TXT record, or your connected Google Analytics/Google & YouTube sales channel - since your hosting changed even if your domain didn't. Submit your updated XML sitemap; Shopify generates one automatically at yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml, and resubmitting it prompts Google to recrawl your new URL structure rather than waiting to stumble onto it. Use the URL Inspection tool to manually request indexing on your highest-value pages - homepage, best-selling products, top blog posts - instead of waiting for Google's natural crawl schedule to reach them.

👉 Run a free demo migration with ShiftItNow and get a clean redirect map to work from.

If Your Domain Changed: Use the Change of Address Tool

When you've moved to a genuinely new domain or subdomain, Google's Change of Address tool (inside Search Console settings) is the correct step - but it comes with two requirements people frequently miss. First, both the old and new domains need to be verified properties in your Search Console account before the tool becomes available. Second, the tool doesn't replace 301 redirects - it depends on them already being fully in place. Submitting a change of address without working redirects underneath it won't transfer your rankings; the redirects do the actual work, and the tool just confirms the move is intentional and permanent.

👉 Talk to a migration expert if your Shopify migration includes a domain change.

Don't Forget Your Google Merchant Center Feed

If you run Google Shopping ads or free product listings, this is the step that gets missed most often. Your product feed is tied to your old platform's URL structure, and if it isn't reconnected, your Shopping listings can start pointing at broken links even while your actual site works fine. Shopify's built-in Google & YouTube sales channel handles feed generation and syncing automatically once connected, which is worth setting up as part of migration day, not as an afterthought once someone notices ad performance dropping.

👉 Migrate with SEO and redirects handled from day one instead of chasing feed issues after launch.

What to Monitor After You Launch

Check Search Console's Coverage report in the first two weeks for a spike in 404 errors - that's your earliest signal a redirect is missing somewhere. Compare the Performance report's impressions and clicks against your pre-migration baseline rather than assuming silence means a problem; some fluctuation while Google recrawls is normal and typically settles within four to eight weeks for a properly redirected migration. Keep an eye on Core Web Vitals too, since site speed can shift when you change platforms, and that affects both rankings and user experience.

Why Most Migration Tools Leave This Part to You

Here's the honest gap: Google Search Console access is tied to you as the site owner, so no migration tool can submit your sitemap or verify your property on your behalf - that part is always manual. But a lot of migration tools don't even hand you a usable starting point, leaving you to build your entire redirect map and figure out your new sitemap structure from scratch, on top of the Search Console work itself. A complete migration tool should generate your 301 redirects and sitemap automatically as part of the migration, so the manual Search Console steps take minutes instead of days.

Quick Post-Migration Google Checklist

  • Confirm whether your move involved a domain change or just a platform change
  • Re-verify your Search Console property using a Shopify-supported method
  • Submit your updated Shopify sitemap (yourdomain.com/sitemap.xml)
  • Use the Change of Address tool only if your domain itself changed, and only after redirects are live
  • Reconnect your Google Merchant Center feed via Shopify's Google & YouTube channel
  • Monitor Coverage and Performance reports weekly for the first month

For the broader picture on ranking risk during a move, see what actually affects your SEO during a Shopify migration, and for what else commonly goes wrong, read our guide on common Shopify migration mistakes.

FAQ: Telling Google About a Shopify Migration

Do I need to use Google's Change of Address tool if I didn't change domains?

No. If your domain stayed the same and only your platform changed, the Change of Address tool doesn't apply - focus on redirects, an updated sitemap, and re-verifying your Search Console property instead.

How long does it take Google to recognize I've moved?

Initial recrawling often begins within days of submitting an updated sitemap, but full stabilization of rankings typically takes four to eight weeks for a properly redirected migration.

Do I need to manually submit every URL to Google?

No. Submitting an updated sitemap and requesting indexing on your highest-priority pages is enough to speed things up - Google will crawl the rest on its normal schedule.

What happens if I forget to update my Google Merchant Center feed?

Your Shopping ads or free listings can end up pointing to broken URLs even if your actual site is working fine, which quietly hurts ad performance until someone catches it.

Can a migration tool submit my sitemap to Google for me?

No - Search Console access is owner-specific, so that step is always manual. A good migration tool can at least generate a clean sitemap and redirect map so the manual submission takes minutes.

Will my Google Business Profile need updating too?

If your website link in Google Business Profile points to an old URL structure, update it to your new Shopify domain or homepage to keep that listing consistent with your actual site.

Telling Google you've moved isn't one universal step - it's a short, specific checklist that depends entirely on whether your domain changed. Get the redirects and sitemap right first, and the Search Console side takes minutes, not days.

Short answer: your visual design doesn't migrate - your content does. That's true no matter which platform you're coming from or which migration tool you use. Products, customer records, orders, blog posts, and pages can transfer to Shopify. The look and feel built in Wix's editor, a Squarespace template, or a custom WordPress theme can't, because Shopify runs on its own completely different theme architecture. That's not a flaw in any particular tool - it's true of every platform migration. Here's what that actually means for your store, and why it's less of a problem than it sounds.

The Honest Answer: Your Design Doesn't Migrate - Your Content Does

Every platform builds its visual layer differently - Wix's drag-and-drop editor, Squarespace's template system, WordPress themes, BigCommerce's Stencil framework - and Shopify uses its own system built on Liquid and, for modern themes, Online Store 2.0's section-and-block structure. There's no technical bridge that translates one platform's design code into another's. What a migration tool moves is the substance: your product data, images, customer accounts, order history, and content. The container that content sits in - your new Shopify theme - is a separate build.

The Two-Track Migration: Data and Design Run in Parallel

The mistake a lot of merchants make is treating design as something to figure out after the data migration finishes. In reality, they're two separate tracks that should run at the same time. Your migration tool handles the data track - products, customers, orders, pages, blog content. Your design track - choosing or building a Shopify theme, setting up navigation, styling your homepage - happens independently, and can start before your data migration is even complete.

Why This Is Actually a Good Opportunity, Not Just Bad News

Shopify's Online Store 2.0 theme framework gives merchants far more section-based flexibility than most legacy platform templates allow, without needing custom code for basic layout changes. Migrating your store is a natural checkpoint to upgrade your design instead of just recreating what you had.

What You Should Carry Over for Brand Consistency

Even with a new theme, your brand shouldn't feel unrecognizable. Bring over your logo files in their original high-resolution format, your brand color palette and fonts as a reference style guide for whoever builds your theme, your existing high-resolution product photography, and the tone and voice of your existing copy. These are the elements that keep returning customers confident they're still shopping with you, even though the layout around them has changed.

What Needs Rebuilding From Scratch

Custom functionality built into your old site - a quiz-style product finder, a custom booking widget, unique page animations, anything built with custom CSS or JavaScript - won't carry over and needs a Shopify app equivalent or custom development. This is closely related to one of the most common Shopify migration mistakes: assuming a plugin or custom feature will just "show up" on the new platform. Auditing your current site's functionality before migration day, not after, is what prevents a feature gap from becoming a launch-day surprise.

Why Most Migration Tools Leave You Guessing on Design

Here's where a lot of merchants get stuck: many migration tools only move product listings and skip your existing pages, blog posts, and navigation structure entirely - which means whoever builds your new theme is starting from a blank slate instead of your actual content. A complete migration tool should bring across your full pages and blog content alongside products, so your new Shopify theme is built around real content from day one instead of placeholder text that gets swapped in later.

Quick Design Migration Checklist

  • Start shopping for a Shopify theme as soon as you commit to migrating, not after data transfer finishes
  • Export your logo, brand colors, fonts, and product photography in their highest resolution
  • Audit custom functionality on your current site and find Shopify app equivalents before launch
  • Make sure your migrated pages and blog content are ready to drop into your new theme's layout
  • Test your new design on mobile specifically, since that's where most traffic and most layout problems show up

FAQ: Store Design and Shopify Migration

Will my website design automatically transfer when I migrate to Shopify?

No. Design and layout are tied to your current platform's theme system and don't transfer to any other platform, including Shopify. Your content - products, pages, blog posts - does migrate.

Can I keep the exact same look on Shopify as my old site?

You can get close by recreating your layout and styling in a Shopify theme, but an exact pixel-for-pixel match usually isn't practical since the underlying theme systems work differently. Most merchants aim for brand consistency rather than an identical copy.

Do I need a developer to build my Shopify theme?

Not necessarily. Shopify's Online Store 2.0 themes are built for merchants to customize without code for most layout and styling needs. A developer becomes useful for custom functionality beyond what a theme's built-in sections support.

Will migrating my content also migrate my page layout?

Content migrates as substance - text, images, structure - but it gets placed into your new theme's layout rather than recreating your old page's exact visual arrangement.

How long does setting up a new Shopify theme take?

It varies widely, from a few days for a simple theme with light customization to several weeks for a fully custom build - which is why it's worth starting in parallel with your data migration rather than after it.

Does changing my design affect my SEO rankings?

Not directly, as long as your content, headings, and URLs are handled correctly during migration. Visual design changes don't hurt rankings - losing content or breaking URLs in the process does.

Your design doesn't move with your data, and that's not a gap in your migration tool - it's just how platform migrations work everywhere. Plan for it as its own project, and you'll come out the other side with a store that looks better than it did before, not just a copy of what you had.

A proper customer account migration should carry across names, email addresses, phone numbers, shipping and billing addresses, order history, marketing consent/opt-in status, and any customer tags or segments you've built up. This isn't a Shopify limitation - it's true everywhere. Passwords are stored as one-way hashes, not as readable text, specifically so that even the platform itself can't see or export them. There's no technical process, migration tool, or workaround that reverses a password hash back into something transferable. Any tool claiming to "migrate" passwords directly either isn't telling you the whole story or is talking about something else entirely, like session tokens.

Here's the part that changes the whole conversation. In February 2026, Shopify officially deprecated its old email-and-password login system for customer accounts. New stores can no longer even enable password-based accounts - every new Shopify store runs on the newer system, where customers log in by entering their email and a one-time six-digit code sent to their inbox. No password to create, remember, or reset. Stores still running the older system continue to work for now, but Shopify has stopped updating it and has confirmed a final shutdown date is coming later in 2026, so building anything new on it isn't worth the risk at this point.

If you specifically need a traditional email-and-password experience preserved - some B2B storefronts prefer it - that's still possible through a third-party authentication app layered on top, but it's no longer Shopify's default, so it needs to be planned for rather than assumed.

A lot of migration tools treat customer accounts as an afterthought - they'll happily move your product catalog and leave customer records as a manual export-and-clean-up job you're expected to handle separately.   • Tell existing customers ahead of launch that sign-in will use an email code instead of a password

Can I migrate customer passwords to Shopify?

No - passwords are stored as irreversible hashes on every platform, including Shopify, so there's no way to transfer them directly. This is true regardless of which migration tool you use.

Will my customers need to reset their passwords after migrating?

If you're on Shopify's current default system, customers won't use a password at all - they'll sign in with their email and a one-time code, so there's no password to reset in the first place.

Not for new stores. As of February 2026, Shopify deprecated password-based login for new customer accounts in favor of email-based one-time codes. Existing stores on the older system still function for now but are no longer being updated.

What happens to customers on Shopify's legacy accounts system?

Existing customer data carries over when you upgrade from the legacy system to the current one - only the sign-in method changes, from a password to an email code.

Will my customers lose their order history when I migrate?

Not if the migration is done properly. Order history should migrate alongside customer accounts as part of a complete migration, not get left behind as a separate step.

Can I keep email + password login on Shopify if I want to?

Yes, through a third-party authentication app layered on top of Shopify's current system - it's no longer the built-in default, so it needs to be set up intentionally rather than assumed.

The number one thing that determines where you land in that range isn't the platform you're coming from — it's how much data you're moving and whether you're using an automated Shopify migration tool or rebuilding by hand.

Typical Shopify Migration Timelines at a Glance

For a small catalog under 500 products with modest customer and order history, the data transfer itself often finishes same-day — sometimes in a couple of hours. A mid-size catalog in the 500 to 5,000 product range typically takes one to three days to fully migrate. Larger or more complex catalogs — 5,000+ products, heavy variant counts, years of order history — can run three to seven days for the data transfer alone. In every case, add planning and testing time on top: even a fast technical migration benefits from a few days of QA before you point your domain at the new store.

What Actually Determines Your Shopify Migration Timeline

Catalog size and variant count are the biggest factors — a product with ten variants takes longer to map correctly than a simple single-SKU item. Customer and order history volume matters too, especially years of historical orders. Content volume — blog posts, static pages, help center articles — adds time if it needs individual redirect mapping. The platform you're migrating from plays a smaller role than people expect: platforms with clean, well-documented APIs generally connect and sync faster than those requiring manual CSV exports, though the difference is usually measured in minutes at the connection stage, not days overall. And by far the biggest swing factor is whether you're using a dedicated migration app or attempting a manual, spreadsheet-based rebuild.

A well-structured Shopify migration breaks into four stages, each with its own rough timeframe. Connect — authorizing access to your current store — usually takes about two minutes. Preview — running a demo migration on a slice of your catalog to confirm everything maps correctly — takes roughly fifteen minutes and is worth every one of them, since it catches mapping issues before they touch your full catalog. Migrate — the full data transfer — is where most of the time budget goes, running anywhere from two hours to three days depending on catalog size, while your original store keeps taking live orders in the background. Launch — the final sync, DNS switch, and going live — typically takes about an hour, ideally with a rollback window afterward in case anything needs a second look.

  • Run a preview/demo migration early enough to fix mapping issues without pressure
  • Schedule the migration for a lower-traffic week, not your busiest sales period
  • Have DNS and domain access ready in advance so the launch step isn't held up waiting on credentials
  • Budget real testing time — checkout, shipping, tax, discount codes — before going fully live
  • Decide who owns go/no-go on launch day ahead of time, so a minor issue doesn't stall the whole timeline while people figure out who makes the call

For catalogs under 500 products, the data transfer itself often finishes in a few hours to a day. Add a few days for testing before you fully launch.

How long does migrating a large catalog take?

posts.meta_description: Worried about losing SEO rankings when you move to Shopify? Here's what actually causes ranking drops during migration — and how to prevent them.
posts.content_html:
Short answer: not if the migration is done correctly. Ranking drops during a platform switch aren't caused by Shopify itself — they're caused by broken URLs, missing redirects, and lost metadata during the move. Google doesn't penalize stores for changing platforms; it penalizes anything that makes previously-ranked pages disappear or become unreachable. If you understand what actually causes SEO damage during a Shopify migration, you can prevent nearly all of it.

Why Rankings Actually Drop During a Migration

Every time you migrate, your URLs almost always change structure, even if only slightly. If those old URLs aren't mapped to their new equivalents, Google's crawler hits a dead end, the page drops out of the index, and the ranking — along with any backlinks pointing to it — goes with it. The other common causes: meta titles and descriptions that don't carry over, image alt text that gets stripped during the move, and structured data (schema) that isn't rebuilt on the new platform. None of these are Shopify's fault — they're migration execution problems.

See how ShiftItNow handles SEO-safe migrations with redirects and metadata built in.

The #1 Factor: 301 Redirects Done Right

If there's one thing that determines whether you keep your rankings, it's this: every old URL needs an individual 301 redirect to its specific new Shopify equivalent — not a blanket redirect dumping every old page onto your new homepage. A blanket redirect tells Google "this specific page no longer exists," which is almost as damaging as no redirect at all. A proper one-to-one redirect map tells Google exactly where each page moved, which passes along the ranking signal instead of resetting it.

Run a free demo migration with ShiftItNow to see your redirect map before anything goes live.

What Else Affects Your SEO During the Move

Beyond redirects, a few other things quietly influence how well your rankings hold up: whether your meta titles and descriptions migrate along with the content (not just the products), whether image alt text survives the move, whether your site speed on Shopify matches or beats your old platform, and whether your XML sitemap gets resubmitted to Google Search Console after launch so Google knows to recrawl the new structure quickly.

Backlinks are worth calling out separately, since they're easy to overlook. Every external site linking to one of your old product or blog URLs is passing along authority to that specific page. If the URL disappears without a redirect, that backlink now points to a dead page instead of your content — you don't just lose the ranking, you lose the value of every link pointing at it too. This is one of the clearest reasons a one-to-one redirect map matters more than people expect going into a migration.

How Long Does It Take for Rankings to Recover?

Even a well-executed migration usually causes some short-term fluctuation — that's Google recrawling and re-indexing your new URLs, not a sign something went wrong. Industry benchmarks generally put full stabilization at around four to eight weeks for a properly redirected migration. What you're watching for during that window is different: temporary fluctuation is normal, but a sustained drop with no recovery signal usually means a redirect or indexing issue that needs fixing, not something to wait out.

Two things speed up that recovery window: submitting your updated sitemap the same day you launch, rather than days later, and manually requesting indexing on your highest-traffic pages through Search Console instead of waiting for Google to discover them on its own schedule.

Talk to a migration expert about protecting your specific rankings before you move.

Why Most Migration Tools Put Your Rankings at Risk

Here's the part that catches merchants off guard: most migration tools only move product data and don't touch redirects, meta tags, or alt text at all — meaning the SEO work is left entirely up to you, after the fact, once rankings have already started slipping. A dedicated Shopify migration app should generate 301 redirects automatically as part of the migration itself, along with migrating your existing meta titles, descriptions, and alt text — not leave SEO as a manual cleanup project you discover you need three weeks after launch.

A Quick SEO Migration Checklist

  • Export a full list of your current URLs before migrating anything
  • Map every old URL to its new Shopify equivalent with a 301 redirect
  • Confirm meta titles, descriptions, and alt text migrated along with content
  • Resubmit your updated XML sitemap in Google Search Console after launch
  • Monitor Search Console for crawl errors and 404s during the first 30 days
  • Keep your old domain/DNS active during the transition rather than shutting it off immediately

Migrate with automatic redirects and metadata preservation instead of rebuilding your SEO from scratch.

If you're weighing this alongside other migration risks, our guide on common Shopify migration mistakes covers the broader list beyond SEO, and our platform guides for Wix, BigCommerce, and Squarespace go deeper on what to expect from your specific platform.

FAQ: SEO and Shopify Migration

Will I definitely lose rankings when I migrate to Shopify?

Not necessarily. Ranking drops come from execution mistakes — missing redirects, lost metadata — not from switching platforms itself. A properly redirected migration typically preserves the large majority of existing rankings.

How long does it take for rankings to stabilize after migration?

Most well-executed migrations stabilize within four to eight weeks as Google recrawls and re-indexes the new URL structure. Some short-term fluctuation during that window is normal.

Do I really need to redirect every single URL, even old blog posts?

Yes. Any indexed page — including old blog posts — can be driving rankings and referral traffic. Skipping redirects on "minor" pages is one of the more common ways migrations lose more SEO value than necessary.

Will moving to Shopify affect my domain authority?

Not directly, as long as you keep your domain and don't introduce a new one. Domain authority is tied to your domain and backlink profile, not your ecommerce platform — the risk comes from broken pages losing the backlinks pointing to them, not the platform switch itself.

Can I keep my blog content and its existing rankings when I migrate?

Every year, thousands of merchants move their stores to Shopify from Wix, BigCommerce, Squarespace, WooCommerce, and half a dozen other platforms — and a lot of them make the same handful of Shopify migration mistakes along the way. Most aren't dramatic failures; they're small oversights that quietly cost weeks of lost SEO rankings, missing customer records, or a checkout flow that breaks on launch day. The good news: nearly every one of these mistakes is avoidable once you know where migrations actually go wrong. Here are the most common Shopify migration errors merchants run into, and exactly how to avoid each one.

Mistake #1: Skipping SEO Redirects

This is the single most damaging — and most common — Shopify migration mistake. When product, collection, and blog URLs change and old links aren't redirected, Google treats every one of those pages as gone. Rankings you spent years building can reset to zero within days. The fix is straightforward: every old URL needs a 301 redirect to its new Shopify equivalent, and your meta titles, descriptions, and image alt text need to migrate along with the content — not just the products themselves.

See how ShiftItNow handles SEO-safe migrations with automatic redirects built in.

Mistake #2: Treating It as a "Products Only" Migration

This is where a lot of merchants get burned. Most migration tools only move product listings, then leave customers, order history, coupons, and content pages behind for you to rebuild by hand — which turns a "quick migration" into weeks of manual data entry. A complete Shopify store migration should carry across customer accounts, full order history, blog posts, and pages in the same pass as your product catalog, not as a separate cleanup project after the fact.

Run a free demo migration with ShiftItNow to see your full store — not just products — mapped before you commit.

Mistake #3: Assuming Customer Passwords Will Transfer

No platform — including Shopify — allows customer passwords to migrate directly, because they're encrypted in ways that can't be reversed or transferred between systems. Merchants who don't plan for this end up fielding a flood of "I can't log in" support tickets right after launch. The fix is simple: set expectations ahead of time and trigger a password reset email for existing customers as part of your launch communication, rather than treating it as a post-launch surprise.

Mistake #4: Skipping a Preview or Demo Migration

Committing to a full migration without previewing it first is one of the riskier Shopify migration mistakes, because you don't find out something mapped incorrectly — variants, categories, custom fields — until it's already live. A short demo migration on a slice of your catalog catches formatting issues while they're still cheap and easy to fix, instead of after your full 5,000-SKU catalog has already moved.

Mistake #5: Migrating During Peak Sales Season

Scheduling a full store migration during Black Friday week or your biggest promotional push is asking for trouble. Even a clean migration involves a short window of final syncing and DNS switching, and if anything needs a second look, you want room to fix it without losing sales. Pick a lower-traffic week, and if possible, run your old and new stores in parallel until you're confident everything checks out.

Talk to a migration expert about the best timing for your store before you schedule anything.

Mistake #6: Forgetting App and Plugin Equivalents

Whatever platform you're coming from, some of your current functionality — reviews, subscriptions, loyalty points, custom checkout logic — was likely powered by a plugin or app that doesn't exist on Shopify in the exact same form. Merchants who don't map these to Shopify equivalents before launch often discover the gap only when a customer complains that a feature is missing. Audit your current app stack before migration day, not after.

Mistake #7: Not Testing the Full Checkout Flow Before Launch

Data can migrate perfectly and a store can still fail on day one if nobody actually tested the buying experience end to end — payment gateways, shipping rates, tax settings, discount codes, and the mobile checkout flow specifically. This is one of the easiest Shopify migration mistakes to avoid and one of the most common to skip simply because everyone's focused on the data migration itself.

Mistake #8: Having No Rollback Plan

Even a well-executed migration can surface an issue after launch — a missing redirect, a miscategorized product batch, a sync error. Merchants who migrate with no way to revert are stuck troubleshooting live, in front of customers. A safety net — a defined rollback window where you can undo the migration if something looks wrong — turns a potential crisis into a minor delay.

Skipping SEO redirects. Without 301 redirects mapping old URLs to new ones, search rankings built up over years can reset almost overnight.

Will my customers' passwords carry over during migration?

No — this is true across every ecommerce platform, not just Shopify. Passwords are encrypted in a way that can't be transferred, so plan on triggering a password reset email as part of your launch communication.

Not usually. Most migration tools only move product listings and leave customers, orders, and content pages for you to migrate manually. A complete migration tool should move your full store — products, customers, orders, blog content, and pages — in one pass.

Should I migrate during a sale or holiday season?

No. Migrating during peak traffic periods increases risk if anything needs troubleshooting. Pick a lower-traffic window and, if possible, keep your old store running in parallel until you've confirmed everything works.

At minimum, run a demo migration on a sample of your catalog and fully test checkout, shipping, tax, and discount codes before pointing your domain at the new store. A few hours of testing can save weeks of post-launch cleanup.

What should I do if something goes wrong after migration?

Have a rollback plan in place before you migrate, not after. A defined rollback window lets you revert quickly if a redirect, sync, or data issue surfaces post-launch, rather than troubleshooting live in front of customers.

Most Shopify migration mistakes come down to the same root cause: treating migration as a simple copy-paste job instead of a full data and SEO transition. Avoid that trap, and moving your store to Shopify can be a smooth, days-long process instead of a weeks-long cleanup project.

4: The Actual Migration Process

This is the biggest step. Here's how it works:

  2. Reformat the CSV to match Shopify's template
  3. Upload to Shopify admin > Products > Import
  4. Manually verify each product (time-consuming)

Time needed: 15 minutes

Pro tip: Do this step last (right before launch). Once you point your domain, your old store goes offline.

Step 5: Set Up 301 Redirects (For SEO)

This protects your search rankings.

Every old URL needs to redirect to the new URL:

  • Old: yourstore.com/products/blue-shoes
  • New: yourstore.com/products/blue-athletic-shoes
  • Redirect: /products/blue-shoes → /products/blue-athletic-shoes

How to do it:

  1. In Shopify admin > Settings > URL Redirects
  2. Add all your old URLs and where they should redirect
  3. Test 5-10 redirects to make sure they work
  4. Google sees the redirects and preserves your rankings

Pro tip: Prioritize product pages and popular blog posts. Don't worry about every single URL.

This is non-negotiable for SEO.

Every old URL must redirect to a new URL. Google sees the redirect and passes ranking authority from the old page to the new page.

Without redirects? Your rankings tank.

How to prioritize redirects:

  • Redirect ALL product pages (these are usually your money pages)
  • Redirect important blog posts
  • Redirect category/collection pages
  • Redirect less important pages (if there's time)

7: Mistakes to Avoid (Learn From Others)

The 5 Biggest Migration Mistakes (And How to Avoid Them)

Mistake #1: Not Backing Up Your Original Data

What happens: You delete your old store after migration. Then something breaks. You panic.

How to avoid it:

  • Export everything from your old store before migration (products, customers, orders, emails)
  • Keep backups in two places (external drive + cloud)
  • Wait 30-60 days before deleting the old store
  • Keep the export files forever (you never know when you'll need them)

Mistake #2: Rushing the Process

What happens: You migrate on a Friday afternoon without testing. Something breaks. No support available. You lose a weekend of sales.

How to avoid it:

  • Plan 2-4 weeks ahead
  • Migrate on a Tuesday-Thursday
  • Test thoroughly before launch
  • Have 24 hours available for monitoring

Mistake #3: Forgetting 301 Redirects

What happens: You lose all your SEO rankings. Traffic disappears. Revenue drops.

How to avoid it:

  • Set up redirects BEFORE pointing your domain
  • Test at least 10 redirects manually
  • Monitor Google Search Console after launch
  • If you see 404s, fix them immediately

Mistake #4: Not Communicating With Customers

What happens: Customers show up and the store looks different. They get confused. Support tickets flood in.

How to avoid it:

  • Email customers 1 week before: "We're moving to a new platform"
  • Email customers day of: "Here's what changed"
  • Email customers day 1 after: "We're here if you have questions"
  • Pin an announcement on your homepage
  • Be responsive to support emails

Mistake #5: Not Testing the Payment System

What happens: You go live. Customers try to buy. Payment processing is broken. You lose sales.

How to avoid it:

  • Test a real transaction in staging first (use a test credit card)
  • Verify payment gateway is connected
  • Check that order confirmation emails send
  • Monitor payments for the first 24 hours
